title: Where new drivers drop off
gist: Priya shows that 38% of new drivers drop off before their first route, with the biggest cliff at the cold location-permission prompt and a second one at email/password login; the goal is to get below 15%.

turns.t: Okay, I think everyone's here. Sofia, you made it, amazing.
Barely. I was on with Brightside until literally one minute ago.
Perfect, that's actually really relevant, so hold that thought. Okay. So. Driver app onboarding. I'm going to share my screen. Can everyone see the Figma? It should say onboarding v2 at the top.
Yep.
Yep, got it.

Cool. So I want to do this in three parts. First the data, like why we're doing this at all, then the actual flow, and then there's a couple of decisions I need from this group, because I can't keep designing around them. So, the data. Thirty-eight percent of new drivers drop off before they complete their first route. So a fleet adds a driver, the driver gets the invite, installs the app, and almost four in ten never actually finish a route in our app. And the target for Q4, the one Asher's been putting in the OKR drafts, is under fifteen.
Under fifteen, yeah. And just to say why I care so much: when drivers don't onboard, the fleet doesn't blame the driver, they blame us. It shows up as the dispatcher saying the app doesn't work.

Exactly. So here's the funnel. This is from the last ninety days, all fleets. Install to account created, we lose about nine points. That's the email and password step. And then the big one. Account created to location permission granted, we lose seventeen points. Seventeen. That's the cliff. Like almost half of the whole drop-off is this one screen. And then the rest is spread out, it's like camera, the first route screen, people who just never come back.
Seventeen on just the permission prompt? Wow.

Yeah. And it makes sense when you look at what we do today. We basically throw the OS prompt at them cold. Right after login, boom, allow Tandem to use your location, and on iOS we're asking for always, which, you know, iOS doesn't even let you ask for always directly anymore. So they get while using the app first, and then later this second prompt pops up in the middle of a route asking to upgrade to always, and people panic and hit don't allow. And then background tracking doesn't work, ETAs go stale for that driver, the dispatcher calls them, it's a mess.
That matches what I hear, honestly. Brightside's dispatchers call it the ghost driver thing. The driver's out on the road but the map shows them sitting at the depot for an hour.
Ghost driver. That's good, I'm stealing that.
And on Android it's not better, right? Background location is its own settings page.

It's worse on Android, kind of. It's a separate trip into settings, and every manufacturer's settings screen looks a bit different. So the second part of the problem is we never explain why. Like, a driver who's never used routing software, why would you let a random app track you all the time? From their point of view that's creepy. Nobody told them it's so the customer gets a right delivery window.
What's the login drop about? Nine points on email and password feels high.

So a few things. A lot of drivers don't have a work email. The fleet enters their personal email, sometimes wrong, and then the invite goes nowhere. And then passwords. We see a lot of password resets in the first week, like a lot. Sofia, you said something about this last time?
Yeah, so Aisha, she's the fleet manager at Brightside, she told me her depot leads keep a notebook. An actual paper notebook with drivers' passwords in it. Because they forget them every morning.
Oh no.
Yeah. So, security-wise, not ideal.
Not ideal. Okay. So that's the why. Questions on the data before I go into the flow?
Just one. Is the thirty-eight percent across all fleets or is it skewed by a couple? Like if one big fleet with a ton of churn is dragging it up.

Good question, I checked. It's skewed a bit by grocery. Grocery fleets are worse, more like forty-five, partly because they hire a lot of seasonal drivers. Parcel is around thirty. But nobody's anywhere near fifteen.
And the ones who drop, do they ever come back? Or are they just gone.
Some come back. About a third of them eventually complete a route, but usually only after a dispatcher calls them or a depot lead sits down with them. So even when it works out, it's support cost.
And a lot of that support cost lands on my team. Onboarding tickets are, I think, the second biggest category in our queue, after ETA questions.
Okay, that's helpful.

title: Walkthrough: phone login, permissions primer, practice route
gist: Priya walks through the new flow: phone-number login with an SMS code, a 3-step permissions primer that explains why each of location (always), notifications and camera is needed, and a practice route in a sandbox.

turns.t: Okay, the flow. So, screen one. This is the big change. No more email and password. You log in with your phone number, we text you a six-digit code, you type it in, you're in. The fleet already has the driver's phone number in most cases because dispatch uses it, so the invite is just a text with a link. Tap the link, it opens the app or the store, and the number's prefilled.
And the code autofills? Because typing six digits with gloves on, that's another drop-off.
Yes, on both platforms, it reads it from the SMS. And then we keep them logged in for, I think we said ninety days, unless the fleet revokes them. So no more morning password ritual. No notebook.
What about shared devices? I know some fleets have like a pool of phones that live in the vans.

Yeah, so that's the edge case. For shared devices the fleet can turn on a switch-driver option, and you log in with your number and the code each shift. It's still way faster than a password. It's maybe, I don't know, five percent of fleets that do shared devices.
Brightside doesn't, for what it's worth. Everyone uses their own phone and they get a stipend.

Okay, good. So, screen two through four. This is the permissions primer. Three steps, one per permission, and each one explains why before we ever show the OS prompt. So step one is location. And the copy is, roughly, your dispatcher and your customers see where you are so they get accurate delivery times, and we only track you while you're on shift. Then there's a little animation of the dot moving along a route and the ETA updating. And then a button that says allow location, and only then do we fire the system prompt. And on iOS we then immediately walk them through the always upgrade with a picture of exactly which option to tap.
Is it true, though? The only on shift part.
It is. Maya, correct me, but we stop the location updates when the route is completed or the driver goes off shift.

Yeah, that's right. We stop publishing. The OS permission is still always, technically, but we're not collecting anything off shift. I'd want legal to look at the exact wording, but the substance is true.

Good, I'll send it to legal. Step two is notifications. Why: your dispatcher can send you route changes and new stops without calling you while you drive. Short. And step three is camera, for proof of delivery photos and scanning barcodes. And camera, we actually ask at the moment you first need it on the practice route, not up front, because it tested better that way.
Tested where? Like with real drivers?

Six drivers. So small. Four from Brightside, two from the Columbus parcel fleet. Sofia set it up. Every one of them got through the location step on the first try in the new flow, and in the current flow, three of the six denied it. Which, it's six people, I'm not going to put that in a board deck, but it's the direction.
One of them said, and I wrote it down, oh, so that's why it wants that. Like it had never occurred to him.

Yeah, that was the moment for me. Okay, and then the last part, the practice route. This is the one that's going to be the most debate, I think. So after permissions, instead of dropping them into an empty home screen waiting for dispatch to assign something, we give them a practice route. It's three to five stops, it's fake, it's in a sandbox, nothing goes to the dispatcher or the customer. And it walks them through the actual mechanics. Start route, navigate to the stop, arrive, scan the package, take the proof of delivery photo, which is where we ask for the camera, mark it delivered, handle a failed delivery, like customer not home. And at the end it says you're ready, and the fleet sees in the dashboard that the driver completed practice.
How long does it take?
About four minutes in testing. Maybe five if someone reads everything.
Okay. That's not bad. I was worried you'd say fifteen.

No, I'm very aware that every minute we add is a minute for them to drop off. But the theory is, the first real route is terrifying, there's a dispatcher watching, there's a van full of groceries, and right now the first time they ever see the scan screen is in front of a customer's door. So we're moving the learning to somewhere safe.
Aisha's basically doing a manual version of this today, for what it's worth. New drivers ride along with a depot lead for half a day before they get their own van.
Which is exactly the thing I'd love to replace with four minutes. Or at least make the half day a lot less painful.
When you say sandbox, what's actually generating the route? Because that's the part where my ears perked up.
I was hoping you'd ask that. Can we come back to it? Because I think it's tied to the skip question, and I want to do those together.
Sure. Yeah. But I'm going to come back to it.
I know you are.
